title: Quantitative trading from scratch to an in-house system
summary: Starting from what a market and a price are, the course teaches how to measure returns and risk, build and honestly test a systematic strategy in Python, and size and control its risk. It then goes deep into pairs trading, factor portfolios, futures and options, machine-learning research, execution and the parts of an in-house trading system, with a project in every module.

concepts.name: A market
concepts.summary: A market matches people who want to buy with people who want to sell, and every match sets a price.

concepts.name: A share
concepts.summary: A share is a slice of a company's ownership that people buy and sell on an exchange.

concepts.name: A quote
concepts.summary: At any moment the best bid is the highest price a buyer offers and the best ask is the lowest price a seller accepts.

concepts.name: The bid-ask spread
concepts.summary: The gap between ask and bid is a cost every immediate trade pays.

concepts.name: A price bar
concepts.summary: A bar summarises all trades in one period by four prices and the volume traded.

concepts.name: A return
concepts.summary: A return measures a gain or loss as a fraction of what you started with.

concepts.name: Compounding
concepts.summary: Returns over several periods combine by multiplying growth factors, so a loss needs a bigger gain to recover.

concepts.name: Log returns
concepts.summary: The logarithm of a growth factor turns multiplying returns into adding them.

concepts.name: Standard deviation
concepts.summary: The standard deviation measures the typical distance of numbers from their mean.

concepts.name: Volatility
concepts.summary: Volatility is the standard deviation of returns, the standard measure of risk.

concepts.name: Annualising
concepts.summary: Average returns scale with time and volatility with the square root of time.

concepts.name: Drawdown
concepts.summary: A drawdown measures how far an account has fallen from its highest value so far.

concepts.name: A benchmark
concepts.summary: Buying once and holding is the benchmark every strategy must beat after costs.

concepts.name: The risk-free rate
concepts.summary: Cash in short government bills earns a nearly safe rate, so a strategy's real gain is its return above it.

concepts.name: The Sharpe ratio
concepts.summary: The Sharpe ratio divides excess return by volatility so strategies with different risk can be compared.

concepts.name: A trading edge
concepts.summary: An edge is a small, repeatable tilt in your favour, and it usually comes from behaviour, risk or market rules.

concepts.name: Strategy families
concepts.summary: Most systematic strategies bet that a move continues, that it reverses, or that holding a risk pays.

concepts.name: Historical price data
concepts.summary: A backtest starts from a table of dated bars, loaded and checked with pandas.

concepts.name: A signal
concepts.summary: A signal is a function from the data known so far to a desired direction or size.

concepts.name: A position
concepts.summary: A position is the signed quantity you hold, and it is what earns returns.

concepts.name: Short selling
concepts.summary: Selling shares you borrowed and buying them back later earns money when the price falls.

concepts.name: Orders
concepts.summary: A market order trades at once at the best price; a limit order waits for a price you name.

concepts.name: Fills
concepts.summary: A fill records the quantity and price an order really got, which can differ from what you asked.

concepts.name: Position sizing
concepts.summary: Sizing turns a signal into a quantity, for example a fixed fraction of the account.

concepts.name: Backtest accounting
concepts.summary: Each bar the books update cash, holdings and equity so every gain and cost is counted once.

concepts.name: The backtest loop
concepts.summary: A backtest repeats one cycle per bar: read data, decide, trade, update the books.

concepts.name: Transaction costs
concepts.summary: Commissions and the spread are paid on every trade, so trading more costs more.

concepts.name: Slippage
concepts.summary: Prices move between decision and fill, so real fills are usually worse than the backtest's.

concepts.name: Look-ahead bias
concepts.summary: A backtest that uses any data not yet known at decision time invents profit.

concepts.name: Adjusted prices
concepts.summary: Splits and dividends break a raw price series, so returns need adjusted prices.

concepts.name: Survivorship bias
concepts.summary: Leaving out companies that failed or were delisted makes any strategy look better.

concepts.name: Out-of-sample testing
concepts.summary: Data used to design a rule cannot judge it; held-back data can.

concepts.name: Multiple testing
concepts.summary: Testing many variants guarantees some look good by chance alone.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.summary: A rule tuned until it matches history's noise fails on new data.

concepts.name: Walk-forward testing
concepts.summary: Walk-forward testing rolls a fit window and a test window forward through time.

concepts.name: The Kelly criterion
concepts.summary: Kelly picks the fraction of capital that maximises long-run growth when the odds are known.

concepts.name: Fractional Kelly
concepts.summary: Because the edge is estimated, betting a fraction of Kelly gives up a little growth for much less risk.

concepts.name: Volatility targeting
concepts.summary: Scaling positions by recent volatility keeps a strategy's risk near a chosen level.

concepts.name: Risk limits
concepts.summary: Hard limits on loss, position size and exposure stop one bad day from ending the strategy.

concepts.name: Is the Sharpe real
concepts.summary: A Sharpe ratio estimated from little data has a wide error, so a result needs enough independent trades.

concepts.name: Stress tests
concepts.summary: Doubling costs, shifting dates and removing the best trades shows how fragile a result is.

concepts.name: A research log
concepts.summary: Recording the idea, every variant tried and every result keeps you honest about multiple testing.

concepts.name: Paper trading
concepts.summary: Running the strategy on live data with simulated fills checks the parts a backtest cannot.

concepts.name: Covariance
concepts.summary: Covariance averages the product of two series' deviations, positive when they move together.

concepts.name: Correlation
concepts.summary: Correlation divides covariance by both volatilities so its size is comparable across pairs.

concepts.name: Stationarity
concepts.summary: A stationary series has a stable mean and spread, so a gap from its mean tends to close.

concepts.name: Cointegration
concepts.summary: Two prices that each wander can still have a combination that is stationary.

concepts.name: Mean-reversion half-life
concepts.summary: The half-life estimates how long a spread takes to close half its distance to the mean.

concepts.name: A pairs trade
concepts.summary: A pairs trade enters when the spread's z-score is far from zero and exits as it reverts.

concepts.name: Borrow costs
concepts.summary: Shorting needs borrowed shares that cost a fee, and a pair can be recalled or squeezed.

concepts.name: Linear regression
concepts.summary: Least squares finds the line that minimises squared vertical distances.

concepts.name: Beta
concepts.summary: Beta is the slope of an asset's returns against the market's, the market risk it carries.

concepts.name: Market-neutral portfolios
concepts.summary: Balancing beta on the long and short side leaves a bet on the spread between them.

concepts.name: Cross-sectional ranking
concepts.summary: Ranking every asset by a measure on the same date turns a signal into relative views.

concepts.name: A factor portfolio
concepts.summary: Sorting assets into groups by a characteristic and going long the top, short the bottom isolates a factor.

concepts.name: Momentum
concepts.summary: Assets that rose most over the past year tend to keep outperforming over the next months.

concepts.name: Mean-variance optimisation
concepts.summary: Combining expected returns and a covariance matrix gives the weights with the best Sharpe ratio.

concepts.name: Shrinkage
concepts.summary: Shrinking estimated returns and covariances toward simple targets stops the optimiser from chasing noise.

concepts.name: A futures contract
concepts.summary: A futures contract fixes a price for a later date, and gains and losses are settled each day.

concepts.name: Rolling futures
concepts.summary: Holding futures for long means rolling into later contracts, and the curve's shape adds or subtracts return.

concepts.name: Option payoffs
concepts.summary: A call pays the rise above a strike at expiry and a put pays the fall below it.

concepts.name: Put-call parity
concepts.summary: A call minus a put equals the stock minus the discounted strike, or someone can lock in free money.

concepts.name: The normal distribution
concepts.summary: The normal distribution describes outcomes built from many small random effects, set by a mean and a standard deviation.

concepts.name: Pricing by replication
concepts.summary: In a one-step model, a mix of stock and cash copies the option, so the option must cost what the mix costs.

concepts.name: The Black-Scholes formula
concepts.summary: Black-Scholes prices a European option from the price, strike, time, rate and volatility.

concepts.name: Delta
concepts.summary: Delta is the change in option value for a small change in the stock price.

concepts.name: Delta hedging
concepts.summary: Rebalancing a stock position to cancel delta leaves a profit or loss driven by realised volatility.

concepts.name: Implied volatility
concepts.summary: Solving Black-Scholes backwards for volatility turns an option price into the market's volatility estimate.

concepts.name: The volatility smile
concepts.summary: Implied volatility varies with strike and expiry because real returns have fat tails and crashes.

concepts.name: The volatility risk premium
concepts.summary: Implied volatility tends to exceed later realised volatility, which option sellers earn with crash risk.

concepts.name: Point-in-time features
concepts.summary: Every feature must use only data published before the decision time, including revisions.

concepts.name: Labels
concepts.summary: A label fixes the target, such as the return over the next ten days or which barrier is hit first.

concepts.name: A classification model
concepts.summary: A classifier such as logistic regression learns from labelled examples to output a probability.

concepts.name: Purged cross-validation
concepts.summary: Overlapping labels leak between folds, so training examples near each test fold are removed.

concepts.name: Sizing from probability
concepts.summary: A position grows with how far the predicted probability is from a coin flip, capped by risk limits.

concepts.name: Signal decay
concepts.summary: Measuring the signal's edge at later horizons shows how quickly it must be traded.

concepts.name: The limit order book
concepts.summary: The book lists resting limit orders at each price, and orders at the same price fill first-come, first-served.

concepts.name: Market impact
concepts.summary: A large order eats through the book, and impact grows roughly with the square root of its size.

concepts.name: Implementation shortfall
concepts.summary: Shortfall compares the price when you decided with the prices you finally got, including what never filled.

concepts.name: TWAP execution
concepts.summary: Time-weighted execution splits an order into equal pieces spread across a period.

concepts.name: VWAP execution
concepts.summary: Volume-weighted execution follows the day's usual volume pattern to hide in the crowd.

concepts.name: Transaction cost analysis
concepts.summary: Comparing fills with benchmarks after the fact splits cost into spread, impact and timing.

concepts.name: The event-driven backtester
concepts.summary: Processing every market and order event in time order lets the same strategy code run in backtest and live.

concepts.name: A market data store
concepts.summary: Storing every observation with when it happened and when you learned it makes point-in-time research possible.

concepts.name: A broker API
concepts.summary: A broker's API accepts orders and reports their states: sent, accepted, partly filled, filled, cancelled.

concepts.name: An order management system
concepts.summary: The order management system compares targets with holdings and open orders, then sends only the difference.

concepts.name: Pre-trade risk checks
concepts.summary: Every order passes size, price and exposure checks, and a kill switch stops everything at once.

concepts.name: Reconciliation
concepts.summary: Comparing your positions and cash with the broker's every day, and alerting on gaps, catches silent failures.
